summary: Updates the IPFIX tcpControlBits Information Element. RFC 7125 revised it for changes to TCP header control bits, but some flag values have since been deprecated, causing interoperability problems. This document removes stale information from the IANA registry and avoids future conflicts. It obsoletes RFC 7125.

eli5.summary: Network reports note which little flags a data packet carried. Some flags went out of use, so this tidies up the list of flags so everyone reads reports the same way.

questions: how are tcp flags exported in ipfix
subtitle: A cleaner IPFIX definition for reporting the TCP flags seen in a network flow, tied to the IANA flags registry.

tldr.problem: RFC 7125's definition of the tcpControlBits element listed flag bits, but a flag value was later deprecated, so that definition risked disagreeing with the authoritative IANA TCP Header Flags registry.
tldr.mechanism: The element definition drops the table of flags and instead points to the IANA registry, refers to flags by bit offset, and requires all observed bits to be exported as seen.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9565 obsoletes RFC 7125, so the registry entry no longer goes stale when TCP flag assignments change.

today: RFC 9565 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 7125, so it is the current definition of the tcpControlBits element.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TCP has a set of control bits, also called flags, for managing connections. The IANA "TCP Header Flags" registry is the authoritative list of assigned bits. RFC 9293 moved it under the TCP Parameters registry, added bits previously specified in RFC 793, removed the NS (Nonce Sum) bit and introduced a "Bit Offset" for each flag in the 16-bit aligned view of the TCP header.

RFC 7125 had revised the IPFIX tcpControlBits Information Element, but a value was deprecated afterwards, so it risked deviating from that registry. RFC 9565 removes stale information from the "IPFIX Information Elements" registry and avoids future conflicts with the TCP registry.

The change also helps observability. For example, operators can spot packets seen with unassigned TCP flags set and work out which applications should be upgraded.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of what each TCP flag means. An older copy of that list had gone out of date, so this document says to look at the official list instead of keeping a copy.

sections.title: The tcpControlBits Element
sections.content:
The element has ElementID 6, the abstract data type unsigned16 and the semantics flags. It reports the TCP control bits observed for the packets of a flow. A bit is set to 1 if any observed packet of the flow had the corresponding TCP bit set, and is 0 otherwise.

The most significant 4 bits of octets 12 and 13 of the TCP header hold the data offset, so those bits MUST be exported as zero and MUST be ignored by the Collector. The tcpHeaderLength element carries that value. All other control bits, including unassigned ones, MUST be exported as observed.

With reduced-size encoding the element covers the low-order octet, bit offsets 8 to 15, and a Collector must not assume anything about bit offsets 4 to 7. An Exporter whose Metering Process cannot observe the flags at offsets 4 to 7 SHOULD use reduced-size encoding.

Earlier revisions required bit offsets 8 and 9 to be exported as zero even if observed. A zero there does not prove the bits were never set, especially if they are zero in every record from a given Exporter.
sections.eli5: It is a row of 16 on-off switches. A switch is on if any packet in the conversation had that flag. A few switches are reserved for another job and must always read off.

sections.title: An Example
sections.content: The RFC shows the element set to 0x92. This reports a flow with CWR (Congestion Window Reduced), ACK and SYN set, which are bit offsets 8, 11 and 14. The registry numbers bits from the most significant bit of octet 12 to the least significant bit of octet 13, but the element is encoded as a regular unsigned 16-bit integer, so implementers have to keep the two views straight.
sections.eli5: If three switches are on, the report says which three, for example the ones for hello, got-it and congestion-slow-down.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA updated the tcpControlBits entry of the "IPFIX Information Elements" registry to repeat the definition in this document. The element's revision number is bumped to 2, and its reference is RFC 9293 and RFC 9565.
sections.eli5: The official list now carries the new, tidier wording.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: TCP control bits may be misused in some flows, for example in DDoS attacks, so an Exporter has to report all observed control bits even when no meaning is attached to a given flag. This is why the document uses stronger requirements language than RFC 7125. It adds no other security considerations beyond those already discussed for IPFIX in RFC 7011.
sections.eli5: Even a flag nobody recognises should be written down, because strange flags can be a sign that someone is up to mischief.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7125
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes:

  • Stale flag bits are no longer mentioned; flags are named by bit offset and the IANA registry is relied on.
  • The table of TCP flag bits is removed from the element description.
  • The registry reference is added to the Additional Information field.
  • Strong normative language is used for exporting observed flags.
  • References are updated, obsolete RFCs are replaced, the revision is bumped and an example section is added.
sections.eli5: Mostly this is a clean-up: the copied list is gone, the wording is firmer, and there is a worked example.
